farina.notes: The sport's first World Champion. Already 43 at the first race; killed in a road accident on the way to the 1966 French GP.

fangio.notes: Titles with four different constructors — Alfa Romeo, Mercedes, Ferrari and Maserati — a feat never repeated. Won 47% of the races he started, still the highest win rate in the sport.

ascari.external_source: F1DB career totals, v2026.19.0; fastest laps from https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alberto_Ascari
ascari.notes: Won every championship race he entered from Belgium 1952 to Belgium 1953, a run that stood as the record until Verstappen in 2023. Killed testing a Ferrari sports car at Monza four days after surviving a plunge into Monaco harbour.

hawthorn.notes: Britain's first World Champion, taken with a single win. Retired immediately after the title and was killed in a road crash on the Guildford bypass three months later.

brabham.notes: The only driver to win the World Championship in a car of his own construction (1966). Pushed his out-of-fuel Cooper over the line to clinch the 1959 title at Sebring.

p-hill.notes: First American World Champion. Took the title at Monza in the race that killed his team-mate von Trips and 15 spectators.

g-hill.notes: The only driver to complete the Triple Crown: Monaco GP, Indianapolis 500 and Le Mans 24 Hours. Five Monaco wins. Killed piloting his own aircraft in fog near Elstree.

clark.notes: Took pole for nearly half his starts. Won the F1 title and the Indianapolis 500 in 1965. Killed in a Formula 2 race at Hockenheim, a death that shook the sport's assumptions about driver invulnerability.

surtees.external_source: F1DB career totals, v2026.19.0; fastest laps from https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Surtees
surtees.notes: The only World Champion on both two wheels and four: seven times on MV Agusta motorcycles, once in a Ferrari. Later ran his own constructor, Team Surtees.

hulme.notes: 'The Bear'. Beat his own employer Jack Brabham to the 1967 title. Died of a heart attack while racing at Bathurst.

stewart.notes: After the titles came a second career as the sport's most consequential safety campaigner — barriers, medical cars, seatbelts, full-face helmets, run-off. Retired one race early after the death of team-mate Cevert.

rindt.notes: The sport's only posthumous World Champion. Killed in practice at Monza; no rival could catch his points total over the remaining races.

fittipaldi.notes: Youngest champion for 33 years at 25. Left McLaren at his peak to run the family Copersucar team, then won the Indianapolis 500 twice.

lauda.notes: Survived catastrophic burns at the Nurburgring in 1976 and returned six weeks later. Later non-executive chairman of Mercedes, where he recruited Hamilton.

hunt.notes: Took the 1976 title by one point in the Fuji rain. Later a famously unvarnished BBC commentator alongside Murray Walker.

andretti.notes: Champion in the ground-effect Lotus 79. Also won the Indianapolis 500, the IndyCar title four times and the Daytona 500 — arguably the most versatile record in motorsport.

scheckter.notes: Ferrari's last champion for 21 years. Retired at 30 and became an organic farmer in Hampshire.

jones.notes: Delivered Williams its first drivers' title and set the template for the team's uncompromising number-one culture.

piquet.notes: First champion of the turbo era (1983). Won titles with both Brabham and Williams.

k-rosberg.notes: Took the 1982 title with a single win in the most turbulent season on record. Father of 2016 champion Nico Rosberg.

prost.notes: 'The Professor' — won by managing races rather than dominating laps. His rivalry with Senna defined the era. Held the win record (51) from 1987 until Schumacher passed it in 2001.

senna.notes: Six Monaco wins including five straight. Killed at Imola on 1 May 1994; the crash triggered the most sweeping safety overhaul in the sport's history.

mansell.notes: Won the title at the 13th attempt in the Williams FW14B, then left for IndyCar and won that championship as a rookie — the only driver to hold both titles simultaneously.

schumacher.notes: Champion with Ferrari every year from 2000 to 2004. Held the record for wins (91) until 2020. Suffered a severe brain injury skiing in December 2013.

d-hill.notes: Son of Graham Hill; the first second-generation World Champion. Dropped by Williams the year he won the title.

villeneuve-j.notes: Son of Gilles Villeneuve. Won the Indianapolis 500 and IndyCar title before arriving in F1 and taking pole on debut at Melbourne.

hakkinen.notes: Survived a life-threatening crash at Adelaide in 1995. Senna named him the rival he rated most highly.

alonso.external_source: formula1.com driver page, 2026-09-04, after round 12 of the 2026 season; fastest laps from F1DB career totals, v2026.19.0
alonso.notes: Ended Schumacher's run in 2005 as the then-youngest champion. Still racing in 2026 at 45; holds the record for most race starts. Also won Le Mans twice and the WEC title.

raikkonen.notes: 'The Iceman'. Took the 2007 title at the last round by one point. Held the record for most race starts (349) until Alonso passed it.

hamilton.external_source: formula1.com driver page, 2026-09-04, after round 12 of the 2026 season; fastest laps from F1DB career totals, v2026.19.0
hamilton.notes: The record holder for wins and poles, and has shared Schumacher's record for titles since 2020. Moved to Ferrari for 2025 and took his first Grand Prix win for them at Barcelona in 2026.

button.notes: Won the 2009 title with Brawn GP in the team's only season.

vettel.notes: Youngest ever World Champion at 23 (2010) and youngest four-time champion. Won every race from Belgium to Brazil in 2013, equalling Ascari's run.

n-rosberg.notes: Beat Hamilton by five points in 2016 and announced his retirement five days later. Son of 1982 champion Keke Rosberg.

verstappen.external_source: formula1.com driver page, 2026-09-04, after round 12 of the 2026 season; fastest laps from F1DB career totals, v2026.19.0
verstappen.notes: Youngest ever F1 starter at 17 and youngest winner at 18. Set single-season records for wins (19) and win percentage in 2023. Won 8 of 24 in 2025 but lost the title to Norris by two points.

norris.external_source: formula1.com driver page, 2026-09-04, after round 12 of the 2026 season; fastest laps from F1DB career totals, v2026.19.0
norris.notes: A first win at Miami in 2024, then the 2025 title by two points from Verstappen with team-mate Piastri third.

moss.notes: Runner-up four consecutive years (1955-58) and third three times. Universally called the greatest driver never to win the championship.

gonzalez.external_source: F1DB career totals, v2026.19.0; fastest laps from https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos%C3%A9_Froil%C3%A1n_Gonz%C3%A1lez
gonzalez.notes: Gave Ferrari its first World Championship Grand Prix win, at Silverstone in 1951.

villoresi.notes: Ascari's mentor and team-mate at Ferrari and Lancia.

taruffi.notes: Won the 1952 Swiss GP; later won the final Mille Miglia in 1957.

trintignant.notes: Two Monaco wins, eight years apart (1955 and 1958).

fagioli.notes: Shared the 1951 French GP win with Fangio at 53, making him the oldest man to win a championship Grand Prix.

brooks.notes: A dentist by training; runner-up in 1959. Moss rated him the fastest of his contemporaries.

collins.notes: Handed his Ferrari to Fangio at Monza in 1956, giving up his own title chance. Killed at the Nurburgring two years later.

musso.notes: Killed at Reims in the 1958 French GP.

bonnier.notes: Gave BRM its first win at Zandvoort in 1959. First chairman of the Grand Prix Drivers' Association.

mclaren-d.notes: Youngest GP winner for 44 years (1959 US GP, aged 22). Founded McLaren in 1963; killed testing a Can-Am car at Goodwood.

von-trips.notes: Leading the 1961 championship when he was killed at Monza along with 15 spectators.

ireland.external_source: F1DB career totals, v2026.19.0; fastest laps from https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Innes_Ireland
ireland.notes: Gave Team Lotus its first championship GP win, at Watkins Glen in 1961.

ginther.notes: Gave Honda its first Grand Prix victory, in Mexico in 1965.

gurney.notes: Won a GP in a car of his own construction (Eagle, Spa 1967) — one of three men to do so, with Jack Brabham and Bruce McLaren. Invented the Gurney flap and the podium champagne spray.

bandini.notes: Died from burns three days after crashing at the Monaco harbour chicane — a crash that drove home the sport's fire-safety failings.

siffert.notes: Killed in a non-championship race at Brands Hatch.

scarfiotti.notes: Last Italian to win the Italian GP for Ferrari, in 1966.

rodriguez-p.notes: Won for Cooper and BRM; a legendary wet-weather driver.

ickx.external_source: F1DB career totals, v2026.19.0; fastest laps from https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacky_Ickx
ickx.notes: Twice championship runner-up; six Le Mans wins. Protested the standing Le Mans start by walking to his car.

regazzoni.notes: Gave Williams its first Grand Prix win at Silverstone in 1979. Paralysed in a crash at Long Beach in 1980.

cevert.notes: Stewart's protege and designated successor at Tyrrell; killed in qualifying at Watkins Glen.

peterson.notes: Twice runner-up. Died of complications after a first-lap crash at Monza, a death that led directly to improved medical response.

reutemann.notes: Lost the 1981 title to Piquet by a point at the final round. Later governor of Santa Fe province.

mass.notes: Won the shortened 1975 Spanish GP at Montjuic, stopped after a fatal accident.

watson.notes: Won from 22nd on the grid at Long Beach in 1983 — still the lowest starting position for a winner.

nilsson.notes: Won the 1977 Belgian GP; died of cancer at 29.

laffite.notes: Career ended by leg injuries in the 1986 British GP startline crash.

jabouille.notes: Won the first Grand Prix for a turbocharged car, at Dijon in 1979.

villeneuve-g.notes: Runner-up in 1979. Killed in qualifying at Zolder. Ferrari has never reissued his number 27 with the same reverence.

pironi.notes: Leading the 1982 championship when leg injuries at Hockenheim ended his career; killed powerboat racing five years later.

arnoux.notes: His 1979 Dijon duel with Villeneuve is among the most replayed pieces of footage in the sport.

de-angelis.notes: Killed testing at Paul Ricard, where the absence of marshals and medical cover caused an outcry.

tambay.notes: Took over Villeneuve's Ferrari seat and won at Hockenheim weeks later.

alboreto.notes: Ferrari's last Italian championship contender, runner-up in 1985. Killed testing an Audi at the Lausitzring.

patrese.notes: Held the record for most Grand Prix starts when he retired; runner-up in 1992.

berger.notes: Won for Benetton, Ferrari and McLaren across three decades of regulations. Survived a fiery crash at Imola in 1989.

boutsen.notes: All his wins came for Williams in 1989-90, two of them in torrential rain.

nannini.notes: Won the 1989 Japanese GP after Senna's disqualification; lost an arm in a helicopter crash in 1990 (later reattached).

alesi.notes: His only win was the 1995 Canadian GP, on his birthday, in a Ferrari.

herbert.notes: Raced on after career-threatening foot injuries in F3000; later an FIA steward.

panis.notes: Won the chaotic 1996 Monaco GP from 14th, with only three cars classified.

frentzen.notes: Championship runner-up in 1997 and third in 1999 with Jordan.

irvine.notes: Lost the 1999 title to Hakkinen by two points while deputising for the injured Schumacher.

coulthard.notes: Runner-up in 2001; the most successful Scottish driver after Clark and Stewart.

barrichello.notes: Held the record for most starts until Raikkonen. Twice runner-up to Schumacher at Ferrari.

r-schumacher.notes: Michael's younger brother; the pair finished 1-2 at the 2001 Canadian GP.

montoya.notes: Won the Indianapolis 500 and CART title before F1, and passed Schumacher around the outside at Interlagos in his first season.

trulli.notes: Won Monaco in 2004. The 'Trulli train' entered the sport's vocabulary.

fisichella.notes: Took Force India's only pole and podium at Spa in 2009.

massa.notes: Lost the 2008 title by one point at his home race, having crossed the line as champion for 38 seconds. Suffered a fractured skull at the Hungaroring in 2009.

webber.notes: Championship runner-up in 2010; later won the World Endurance Championship with Porsche.

kubica.notes: Poland's only GP winner (Canada 2008). Returned to F1 in 2019 after a rally crash partially severed his forearm.

kovalainen.notes: Won the 2008 Hungarian GP for McLaren.

maldonado.notes: Williams's only win between 2004 and 2012, at Barcelona in 2012.

ricciardo.notes: Won for Red Bull and McLaren, several times from improbable positions.

bottas.notes: Championship runner-up as Hamilton's Mercedes team-mate. Returned to a race seat with Cadillac in 2026.

perez.notes: Won Monaco in 2022; runner-up in 2023. Returned with Cadillac in 2026.

gasly.notes: Won the 2020 Italian GP for AlphaTauri, the team's second and last victory.

ocon.notes: Won the 2021 Hungarian GP for Alpine.

leclerc.external_source: formula1.com driver page, 2026-09-04, after round 12 of the 2026 season
leclerc.notes: Ferrari's lead driver since 2019; won his home Monaco Grand Prix in 2024. Championship runner-up in 2022.

sainz.notes: Won for Ferrari at Silverstone 2022, Singapore 2023 and Melbourne 2024. Son of the double World Rally Champion.

russell.external_source: formula1.com driver page, 2026-09-04, after round 12 of the 2026 season; poles from https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/George_Russell_(racing_driver)
russell.notes: First win at Interlagos 2022. Won twice in 2025 and again in Australia and Austria in 2026. GPDA director.

piastri.external_source: formula1.com driver page, 2026-09-04, after round 12 of the 2026 season
piastri.notes: Won races in 2025 and finished third in the championship.

antonelli.notes: Promoted to Mercedes at 18 to replace Hamilton. Leads the 2026 championship.

hulkenberg.notes: Took pole for Williams in 2010; a first podium came at Silverstone in 2025. Won Le Mans outright in 2015.

albon.notes: Podiums with Red Bull in 2020; Williams's lead driver since 2022.

stroll.notes: Front row at Monza in 2017; pole at Istanbul in 2020.

tsunoda.notes: Promoted to Red Bull for 2025; reserve and substitute duties with Racing Bulls in 2026.

hadjar.notes: Rookie of 2025 with Racing Bulls; promoted to Red Bull alongside Verstappen for 2026.

lawson.notes: Racing Bulls race driver in 2026 after a brief 2025 stint at Red Bull.

bearman.notes: Scored on debut standing in for Sainz at Ferrari in Jeddah 2024; Haas race driver since 2025.

colapinto.notes: Argentina's first F1 racer since 2001; Alpine race driver in 2026.

bortoleto.notes: F3 and F2 champion in consecutive years before reaching F1 with Sauber, now Audi.

lindblad.notes: Red Bull junior promoted to Racing Bulls for 2026.

doohan.notes: Alpine race driver at the start of 2025. Son of five-time 500cc champion Mick Doohan.

grosjean.notes: Survived a 67 g impact and 28 seconds in the fire at Bahrain in 2020 — the crash that vindicated the halo.

bianchi.notes: Scored Marussia's only points. Died from injuries sustained at Suzuka in 2014, the first F1 fatality from an on-track accident since 1994; his death led to the virtual safety car and the halo programme.

de-villota.notes: Marussia test driver; sustained fatal-course injuries in a straight-line test accident in 2012.

wolff-s.notes: Williams development driver; first woman to take part in an F1 race weekend in 22 years (2014). Managing Director of F1 Academy.

lombardi.notes: The only woman to score in a World Championship Grand Prix — half a point for sixth at the shortened 1975 Spanish GP.

beltoise.notes: Won the 1972 Monaco Grand Prix for BRM in torrential rain — the team's last victory. Raced with a permanently weakened left arm after a sports-car crash.

gethin.notes: Won the 1971 Italian Grand Prix by 0.01 seconds — the closest finish in the sport's history, with the top five covered by 0.61 s.

brambilla.notes: 'The Monza Gorilla'. Won the rain-shortened 1975 Austrian Grand Prix for March and crashed on the slowing-down lap while waving to the crowd.

pace.notes: Won his home Grand Prix at Interlagos in 1975 for Brabham. Killed in a light-aircraft crash; the Interlagos circuit is named after him.

baghetti.notes: Won the 1961 French Grand Prix at Reims in his first World Championship race. Only Nino Farina and Johnnie Parsons, both in the championship's first season, had done the same, and nobody has since.

parsons.notes: Won the Indianapolis 500 in the years it counted towards the Formula One World Championship (1950-1960). Recorded as a World Championship race winner in the official record; did not contest European Grands Prix.

bas-leinders.notes: The 1998 German Formula Three champion, and Minardi's test and reserve driver in 2004, running on Grand Prix Fridays.

bjorn-wirdheim.notes: The 2003 International Formula 3000 champion, and Jaguar's third driver in 2004, doing the team's Friday running at Grand Prix weekends.

ryan-briscoe.notes: The 2003 Formula Three Euroseries champion and a Toyota test driver since 2002, who became the team's Friday third driver for the last part of 2004.

chanoch-nissany.notes: An Israeli real-estate developer who became Minardi's official test driver for 2005, and the first Israeli to take part in a Grand Prix weekend.

enrico-toccacelo.notes: Runner-up in the 2004 International Formula 3000 championship, and Minardi's third driver on Grand Prix Fridays from the 2005 Turkish Grand Prix.

alexandre-premat.notes: A GP2 driver with ART Grand Prix and A1 Team France's driver, who ran the third Spyker MF1 car at the 2006 Chinese Grand Prix.

ernesto-viso.notes: A GP2 driver who ran the third Spyker MF1 car in Friday practice at the 2006 Brazilian Grand Prix.

giorgio-mondini.notes: The 2004 Formula Renault V6 Eurocup champion, and one of Midland's third drivers in 2006.

michael-ammermuller.notes: A Red Bull junior racing in GP2 for Arden, promoted to Red Bull Racing's third driver for the end of the 2006 season.

neel-jani.notes: A GP2 driver in 2005 and A1 Team Switzerland's driver, and Scuderia Toro Rosso's third driver throughout 2006.

fairuz-fauzy.notes: Lotus Racing's third driver in 2010, having been one of Spyker's test and reserve drivers.

davide-valsecchi.notes: A GP2 driver confirmed as Team Lotus's test driver in 2011, who took Heikki Kovalainen's car in Friday practice at the Malaysian Grand Prix.

jan-charouz.notes: The 2009 Le Mans Series champion and Renault's reserve driver in 2010, who took Vitantonio Liuzzi's car for first practice at the last round of 2011.

luiz-razia.notes: A GP2 driver with Team AirAsia, and Team Lotus's reserve and test driver in 2011, having tested for Virgin Racing.

robert-wickens.notes: GP3 runner-up in 2010 and Formula Renault 3.5 champion in 2011, the year Virgin Racing signed him as its reserve driver.

dani-clos.notes: HRT's test driver for 2012, while racing in GP2 for Barwa Addax.

ma-qinghua.notes: A member of HRT's development programme who became, in 2012, China's first driver in a Grand Prix practice session, and Caterham's Friday test driver the following year.

james-calado.notes: A GP2 driver with ART Grand Prix and the 2011 GP3 runner-up, whom Force India chose as its third driver for the 2013 Italian Grand Prix.

rodolfo-gonzalez.notes: A GP2 driver, with Caterham Racing in 2012, named Marussia's reserve driver for 2013.

adderly-fong.notes: A Hong Kong driver racing in GP3 with Jenzer Motorsport in 2014, the year he tested for Sauber.

daniel-juncadella.notes: Winner of the Macau Grand Prix and a Formula 3 champion before he joined Force India as its reserve driver in 2014.

robin-frijns.notes: The 2012 Formula Renault 3.5 champion and formerly Sauber's test and reserve driver, who became Caterham's reserve driver in 2014.

fabio-leimer.notes: The 2013 GP2 champion, signed as Manor Marussia's reserve driver for 2015.

raffaele-marciello.notes: The 2013 FIA Formula 3 European champion, who had raced in GP2, signed as Sauber's test and reserve driver for 2015.

alfonso-celis-jr.notes: A former GP3 driver, signed by Force India as its development and free practice driver for 2016.

jordan-king.notes: A GP2 driver signed as Manor's development driver for 2015 and kept on for 2016, the year he drove for the team in Friday practice.

sean-gelael.notes: Toro Rosso's test driver in 2017 and 2018, racing in Formula 2 for Pertamina Arden and then Prema.

artem-markelov.notes: Renault's development driver in 2018, racing in Formula 2 for Russian Time.

naoki-yamamoto.notes: A Honda driver who won both the Super Formula and the Super GT GT500 titles in 2018, and drove for Toro Rosso in first practice at the 2019 Japanese Grand Prix.

roy-nissany.notes: Williams' official test driver in 2020 and 2021, racing in Formula 2 for Trident and then DAMS; the son of Chanoch Nissany.

callum-ilott.notes: Runner-up in the 2020 Formula 2 Championship, then Ferrari's test driver and a reserve for Alfa Romeo in 2021.

alex-palou.notes: The 2021 IndyCar champion with Chip Ganassi Racing, and a reserve driver for McLaren in 2022.

felipe-drugovich.notes: The 2022 Formula 2 champion, taken on by Aston Martin as a reserve driver and the first member of its driver development programme.

juri-vips.notes: A Red Bull junior racing in Formula 2, and one of Red Bull's reserve drivers in 2022.

patricio-oward.notes: The 2018 Indy Lights champion, racing in IndyCar for McLaren's team there, and one of McLaren's Formula One reserve drivers.

robert-shwartzman.notes: The 2019 FIA Formula 3 champion and a Ferrari reserve driver, having finished second in Formula 2 with Prema in 2021.

theo-pourchaire.notes: A Sauber junior and Alfa Romeo's reserve driver for 2023, runner-up in Formula 2 in 2022 and leading the 2023 Formula 2 championship into its final round.

frederik-vesti.notes: A Mercedes junior, runner-up in Formula 2 in 2023, who became the team's reserve driver in 2024.

jake-dennis.notes: The 2022-23 Formula E champion with Andretti, and Red Bull's simulator and development driver.

zak-osullivan.notes: Second in FIA Formula 3 in 2023, and a member of the Williams Driver Academy.

arthur-leclerc.notes: Ferrari's development driver, who had raced in Formula 2 with DAMS; the younger brother of Charles Leclerc.

ayumu-iwasa.notes: A Red Bull junior from Honda's Formula Dream Project, who moved from Formula 2 to Super Formula and won its title in 2025.

luke-browning.notes: A member of the Williams Driver Academy, who came up through FIA Formula 3 into Formula 2.

alexander-dunne.notes: A McLaren junior, racing in Formula 2 for Rodin Motorsport in 2025.

antonio-fuoco.notes: A Ferrari factory driver in the World Endurance Championship, winner of the 2024 24 Hours of Le Mans, and a development driver for Ferrari's Formula One team.

cian-shields.notes: Runner-up in the 2023 Euroformula Open Championship and a Hitech driver in FIA Formula 3 in 2024, given Fernando Alonso's Aston Martin for a Friday session.

dino-beganovic.notes: A member of the Ferrari Driver Academy racing in Formula 2, whom Ferrari put in Charles Leclerc's car for Friday practice.

jak-crawford.notes: A member of Aston Martin's driver development programme, runner-up in Formula 2 with DAMS in 2025, and the team's reserve driver.

paul-aron.notes: A former Mercedes junior, third in Formula 2 in 2024, who joined Alpine as its reserve driver and ran Friday sessions for Sauber as well.

victor-martins.notes: The 2020 Formula Renault Eurocup and 2022 FIA Formula 3 champion, and Williams' test and development driver.

colton-herta.notes: An IndyCar driver from 2018 to 2025, who moved to Formula 2 with Hitech in 2026 as Cadillac's Formula One test driver.

leonardo-fornaroli.notes: The 2024 FIA Formula 3 and 2025 Formula 2 champion, and McLaren's reserve driver in 2026.
